title: Energy-Conditioned Noise Schedule and Whitening for Spectral Diffusion

paper.title: Energy-Conditioned Noise Schedule and Whitening for Spectral Diffusion
paper.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces an energy-adaptive noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models. Existing spectral diffusion methods account for the non-uniform statistics of transform coefficients through coefficient scaling, normalization, or frequency prioritization, while the forward diffusion noise schedule remains largely independent of the underlying spectral-energy distribution. We investigate whether the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process should also follow the spectral organization of natural images. The proposed formulation combines global spectral whitening with energy-conditioned noise allocation that jointly modulates the injected noise according to the energy of individual transform coefficients and an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time. The resulting forward process preserves Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals and remains compatible with standard DDPM and DDIM procedures without modifying the diffusion architecture. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the contribution of the proposed energy-conditioned noise schedule and spectral whitening, reducing Fréchet Inception Distance from 142.48 for a compact DCTdiff U-Net variant to 100.45.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Denoising diffusion models [ 11 , 6 , 12 ] formulate image generation as the reverse of a stochastic process that progressively transforms data into Gaussian noise. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [ 6 ] and Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) [ 12 ] provide stochastic and deterministic realizations of this principle, respectively, while continuous-time formulations have been investigated in [ 13 ] . Most existing diffusion models operate directly on pixel representations, where the forward diffusion process applies an identical noise schedule to every image coordinate. Recently, several studies have investigated diffusion in transform-domain representations, including the Fourier [ 2 , 3 ] and discrete cosine transform (DCT) [ 1 ] domains [ 8 , 4 ] . Unlike pixel representations, transform coefficients possess well-defined spectral meaning and exhibit highly non-uniform statistical properties. In natural images, most of the signal energy is concentrated in a relatively small number of low-frequency DCT coefficients, whereas higher-frequency components contain substantially less energy. Consequently, the transform domain is characterized by a pronounced imbalance between spectral components. Recent transform-domain diffusion models explicitly account for this imbalance. DCTDiff [ 8 ] introduces coefficient scaling, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scaling, and frequency prioritization to improve optimization in the DCT domain. Moreover, the authors show that image diffusion exhibits a spectral autoregressive behavior, indicating that transform coefficients contribute unequally throughout the diffusion process. These observations suggest that spectral diffusion fundamentally differs from pixel-domain diffusion and should exploit the underlying spectral organization of natural images. Motivated by these observations, we investigate a complementary question that, to the best of our knowledge, has not been addressed previously: should the forward diffusion noise schedule itself depend on the spectral-energy distribution? Existing transform-domain diffusion methods adapt the representation, coefficient scaling, or optimization strategy, whereas the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process remains largely independent of the spectral energy associated with individual transform coefficients. This paper introduces an energy-conditioned noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models. Rather than proposing a new diffusion architecture, the objective is to investigate spectral-energy-aware noise scheduling as an independent component of existing transform-domain diffusion frameworks. The proposed schedule depends on diffusion time, coefficient energy, and image-dependent spectral energy, assigning smaller perturbations to dominant spectral components while modulating their temporal evolution according to the spectral-energy distribution of each image. The resulting formulation preserves the standard Gaussian diffusion framework and remains directly compatible with conventional DDPM and DDIM training and sampling procedures. To isolate the contribution of the proposed scheduling strategy, the experimental evaluation employs the same U-Net architecture and identical training configuration with both uniform and energy-conditioned spectral noise schedules. The objective is not to compare different diffusion architectures, but to evaluate the influence of energy-conditioned scheduling within the same transform-domain diffusion framework. The proposed formulation is presented in Section 3 , its relation to DCTdiff is discussed in Section 4 , and the experimental evaluation is given in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 2 Baseline Spectral Diffusion Framework
sections.text: This section introduces the baseline transform-domain diffusion framework adopted throughout this work. Following the JPEG coding pipeline [ 16 ] and the block-DCT representation introduced in DCTdiff [ 8 ] , the image is converted into compact spectral coefficients before diffusion. Unlike DCTdiff, which employs a Transformer backbone, the present work uses the resulting spectral representation as the input to a conventional U-Net diffusion model. This baseline serves as the reference framework upon which the proposed Energy-Conditioned Spectral Diffusion (ECSdiff) is introduced in the next section.

sections.heading: 3 Energy-Conditioned Spectral Diffusion
sections.text: The baseline framework described in the previous section follows the standard DDPM formulation with a uniform forward noise schedule. Recent theoretical analysis of transform-domain diffusion has shown that the diffusion process inherently exhibits spectral autoregressive behavior, whereby high-frequency components progressively lose their signal-to-noise ratio earlier than low-frequency components under isotropic Gaussian perturbations [ 8 ] . This behavior follows directly from the power-law energy profile of natural images and provides a theoretical justification for treating individual spectral components differently during diffusion. Rather than modifying the diffusion architecture, the proposed ECSdiff explicitly incorporates this observation into the forward process by introducing an energy-conditioned noise schedule. The proposed formulation consists of three consecutive stages. First, the compact spectral representation is whitened to reduce the statistical imbalance between spectral components. Second, the spectral-energy distribution is estimated from the original transform coefficients. Finally, the forward noise schedule is modulated according to the estimated spectral energy.

sections.heading: 4 Relation to DCTdiff
sections.text: Figure 1: Radial DCT energy profile in the YCbCr and RGB domains for the full-spectrum representation. ECSdiff introduces a spectral diffusion strategy that advances the DCTdiff philosophy [ 8 ] while retaining its baseline framework defined in Section 2 . DCTdiff compensates for spectral imbalance through Entropy-Consistent Scaling (ECS), Entropy-Based Frequency Reweighting (EBFR), and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scaling. ECS applies a common factor η \eta to all retained coefficients, x k ′ = x k / η x_{k}^{\prime}=x_{k}/\eta , whereas EBFR weights the denoising objective according to the entropy of individual frequency distributions. Since ECS moves low-energy coefficients closer to zero, DCTdiff additionally scales the SNR of the default noise schedule to compensate for their earlier corruption. Our strategy replaces global scaling with component-wise normalization x ~ k = x k / s k \tilde{x}_{k}=x_{k}/s_{k} ( 5 ). The resulting spectral statistics are further incorporated through the factors ψ k \psi_{k} ( 8 ) and β E ( i ) ​ ( t ) \beta_{E}^{(i)}(t) ( 11 ), defining the coefficient- and image-dependent schedule β k , t ( i ) = β t ​ β E ( i ) ​ ( t ) ​ ψ k \beta_{k,t}^{(i)}=\beta_{t}\beta_{E}^{(i)}(t)\psi_{k} ( 12 ). Hence, spectral statistics directly control normalization and noise allocation. This formulation is consistent with the spectral autoregression established by Theorem 5.1 in [ 8 ] , according to which isotropic diffusion noise first corrupts low-energy high-frequency components and progressively affects lower frequencies. DCTdiff exhibits this ordering implicitly, whereas the proposed schedule explicitly incorporates spectral energy into the forward process through β k , t ( i ) \beta_{k,t}^{(i)} . A further distinction arises during sampling. Since the energy-conditioned β k , t ( i ) \beta_{k,t}^{(i)} path is image-dependent, it is retained in the reverse process, allowing sampling to follow the spectral-energy characteristics of the conditioning image and potentially benefit conditioned image generation. sections.heading: 5 Experimental Verification and Analysis
sections.text: The experimental analysis considers two spectral diffusion settings: (i) full-spectrum DCT diffusion to examine the limitations of uniform spectral diffusion models (USDM), and (ii) compact block-DCT diffusion for evaluating the proposed ECSdiff and its comparison with DCTdiff [ 8 ] under a common experimental setting.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Experiments are conducted on CIFAR-10 using the standard training and test partitions of respectively 50,000 50{,}000 and 10,000 10{,}000 RGB images with a resolution of 32 × 32 32\times 32 . For direct comparison, the DCTdiff framework is adapted from its original transformer-based implementation to the same U-Net backbone used by ECSdiff, while preserving its spectral representation and diffusion procedure. This provides a common, lower-capacity setting for evaluating the effect of the proposed energy-conditioned modifications. All models use T = 1000 T=1000 diffusion steps and are evaluated using both DDPM and DDIM sampling. A Python implementation of ECSdiff is available at [ 15 ] . sections.heading: 5.2 Full-Spectrum DCT Diffusion
sections.text: The first experiment evaluates direct full-spectrum DCT diffusion, without the block-DCT organization and coefficient reduction defined in ( 1 ) and ( 2 ). This setting preserves the full spectral imbalance and therefore provides a demanding case for evaluating the proposed conditioning. The transition from the pixel domain to the full DCT representation produces a highly non-uniform spectral-energy profile dominated by low-frequency coefficients, as shown in Fig. 1 . Applying the ECSdiff normalization ( 5 ) and spectral weighting ( 6 ) to the full-spectrum representation reduces this imbalance and produces a more compact coefficient profile centered around zero, as shown in Fig. 2 .

sections.heading: 5.4 Ablation Analysis
sections.text: The ablation analysis isolates the contribution of spectral whitening and energy-conditioned noise scheduling within the compact spectral framework. Starting from USDM, the EAFW configuration introduces dataset-level spectral whitening, while ECSdiff additionally incorporates the image-dependent energy-conditioned noise schedule. At 1000 1000 epochs, USDM achieves an FID of 192.2413 192.2413 , while DCTdiff achieves 176.6944 176.6944 . Introducing spectral whitening in EAFW further reduces the FID to 152.7026 152.7026 , and adding the energy-conditioned noise schedule reduces it to 136.6838 136.6838 for ECSdiff. These results support the dataset-level whitening in ( 5 ) as a mechanism for reducing systematic differences between spectral modes, while preserving image-specific energy variations used by β E ( i ) ​ ( t ) \beta_{E}^{(i)}(t) .

sections.heading: 5.5 Sampling Performance
sections.text: The sampling performance is evaluated using both DDPM and DDIM to examine the visual behavior of the spectral diffusion models after 1000 1000 training epochs. USDM DCTdiff EAFW ECSdiff Figure 5: Sampling comparison after 1000 1000 training epochs using the same seed from the test set for all methods. From left to right: USDM, DCTdiff, EAFW, and ECSdiff. Upper row: DDPM sampling. Lower row: DDIM sampling ( 14 ). Figure 5 shows the sampling behavior of USDM and DCTdiff and isolates the effect of energy-conditioned diffusion by comparing EAFW and ECSdiff. ECSdiff produces coherent object structures under both DDPM and DDIM sampling. Compared with EAFW, the main differences are observed in spectral amplitude and color contrast rather than object structure. The corresponding FID results show improved distributional similarity for ECSdiff, while the visual comparison indicates that the energy-conditioned noise schedule also affects contrast and chrominance.

sections.heading: 5.6 Discussion
sections.text: The results distinguish the roles of the energy-conditioned components. Global spectral whitening provides dataset-level normalization while preserving image-dependent energy variations. The effect of ψ k \psi_{k} is primarily learned during training: using the ECSdiff-trained model with the EAFW sampling configuration confirms that it need not be reapplied during sampling. Setting ψ k = 1 \psi_{k}=1 improves FID at almost all evaluated checkpoints, reaching 100.45 100.45 with 10000 10000 samples compared with 106.55 106.55 when ψ k \psi_{k} is retained. The variability observed with 1000 1000 samples (Figure 4 ) is therefore largely attributed to the limited FID sample size. In contrast, the image-dependent β E ( i ) ​ ( t ) \beta_{E}^{(i)}(t) path remains relevant for energy-conditioned training and potentially provides a more important conditioning mechanism during sampling. The gradual introduction of higher spectral weights ω \omega over diffusion steps t t and training epochs e e ( 6 ), together with the epoch-dependent learning rate lr ⁡ ( e ) \mathrm{lr}(e) , improves optimization and accelerates convergence during the early training epochs. Future experiments will extend ECSdiff to transformer-based architectures and larger training datasets with higher-resolution images, such as ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution, to examine whether the improvements demonstrated here with the compact DCTdiff architecture are preserved across different spectral diffusion models.

Speedway Blvd., city=Tucson, postcode=85721-0104, state=AZ, country=USA Abstract This paper introduces an energy-adaptive noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models. Existing spectral diffusion methods account for the non-uniform statistics of transform coefficients through coefficient scaling, normalization, or frequency prioritization, while the forward diffusion noise schedule remains largely independent of the underlying spectral-energy distribution. We investigate whether the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process should also follow the spectral organization of natural images. The proposed formulation combines global spectral whitening with energy-conditioned noise allocation that jointly modulates the injected noise according to the energy of individual transform coefficients and an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time. The resulting forward process preserves Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals and remains compatible with standard DDPM and DDIM procedures without modifying the diffusion architecture. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the contribution of the proposed energy-conditioned noise schedule and spectral whitening, reducing Fréchet Inception Distance from 142.48 for a compact DCTdiff U-Net variant to 100.45. keywords Diffusion models,Spectral diffusion,Energy-conditioned noise scheduling,Transform-domain diffusion,Spectral whitening † † titlenote: Bane Vasic acknowledges the support of the National Science Foundation under grant CCF-2100013, and a generous gift from his friends and Maecenases Dora and Barry Bursey. † † credit: Conceptualization of this study, Methodology, Software † † credit: Methodology, Supervision † † corresponding: Corresponding author 1 Introduction Denoising diffusion models [ 11 , 6 , 12 ] formulate image generation as the reverse of a stochastic process that progressively transforms data into Gaussian noise. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [ 6 ] and Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) [ 12 ] provide stochastic and deterministic realizations of this principle, respectively, while continuous-time formulations have been investigated in [ 13 ] . Most existing diffusion models operate directly on pixel representations, where the forward diffusion process applies an identical noise schedule to every image coordinate. Recently, several studies have investigated diffusion in transform-domain representations, including the Fourier [ 2 , 3 ] and discrete cosine transform (DCT) [ 1 ] domains [ 8 , 4 ] . Unlike pixel representations, transform coefficients possess well-defined spectral meaning and exhibit highly non-uniform statistical properties. In natural images, most of the signal energy is concentrated in a relatively small number of low-frequency DCT coefficients, whereas higher-frequency components contain substantially less energy. Consequently, the transform domain is characterized by a pronounced imbalance between spectral components. Recent transform-domain diffusion models explicitly account for this imbalance. DCTDiff [ 8 ] introduces coefficient scaling, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scaling, and frequency prioritization to improve optimization in the DCT domain. Moreover, the authors show that image diffusion exhibits a spectral autoregressive behavior, indicating that transform coefficients contribute unequally throughout the diffusion process. These observations suggest that spectral diffusion fundamentally differs from pixel-domain diffusion and should exploit the underlying spectral organization of natural images. Motivated by these observations, we investigate a complementary question that, to the best of our knowledge, has not been addressed previously: should the forward diffusion noise schedule itself depend on the spectral-energy distribution? Existing transform-domain diffusion methods adapt the representation, coefficient scaling, or optimization strategy, whereas the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process remains largely independent of the spectral energy associated with individual transform coefficients. This paper introduces an energy-conditioned noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models. Rather than proposing a new diffusion architecture, the objective is to investigate spectral-energy-aware noise scheduling as an independent component of existing transform-domain diffusion frameworks. The proposed schedule depends on diffusion time, coefficient energy, and image-dependent spectral energy, assigning smaller perturbations to dominant spectral components while modulating their temporal evolution according to the spectral-energy distribution of each image. The resulting formulation preserves the standard Gaussian diffusion framework and remains directly compatible with conventional DDPM and DDIM training and sampling procedures. To isolate the contribution of the proposed scheduling strategy, the experimental evaluation employs the same U-Net architecture and identical training configuration with both uniform and energy-conditioned spectral noise schedules. The objective is not to compare different diffusion architectures, but to evaluate the influence of energy-conditioned scheduling within the same transform-domain diffusion framework. The proposed formulation is presented in Section 3 , its relation to DCTdiff is discussed in Section 4 , and the experimental evaluation is given in Section 5 . 2 Baseline Spectral Diffusion Framework This section introduces the baseline transform-domain diffusion framework adopted throughout this work. Following the JPEG coding pipeline [ 16 ] and the block-DCT representation introduced in DCTdiff [ 8 ] , the image is converted into compact spectral coefficients before diffusion. Unlike DCTdiff, which employs a Transformer backbone, the present work uses the resulting spectral representation as the input to a conventional U-Net diffusion model. ECSdiff introduces a spectral diffusion strategy that advances the DCTdiff philosophy [ 8 ] while retaining its baseline framework defined in Section 2 . DCTdiff compensates for spectral imbalance through Entropy-Consistent Scaling (ECS), Entropy-Based Frequency Reweighting (EBFR), and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scaling. ECS applies a common factor η \eta to all retained coefficients, x k ′ = x k / η x_{k}^{\prime}=x_{k}/\eta , whereas EBFR weights the denoising objective according to the entropy of individual frequency distributions. Since ECS moves low-energy coefficients closer to zero, DCTdiff additionally scales the SNR of the default noise schedule to compensate for their earlier corruption. Our strategy replaces global scaling with component-wise normalization x ~ k = x k / s k \tilde{x}_{k}=x_{k}/s_{k} ( 5 ). The resulting spectral statistics are further incorporated through the factors ψ k \psi_{k} ( 8 ) and β E ( i ) ​ ( t ) \beta_{E}^{(i)}(t) ( 11 ), defining the coefficient- and image-dependent schedule β k , t ( i ) = β t ​ β E ( i ) ​ ( t ) ​ ψ k \beta_{k,t}^{(i)}=\beta_{t}\beta_{E}^{(i)}(t)\psi_{k} ( 12 ). Hence, spectral statistics directly control normalization and noise allocation. This formulation is consistent with the spectral autoregression established by Theorem 5.1 in [ 8 ] , according to which isotropic diffusion noise first corrupts low-energy high-frequency components and progressively affects lower frequencies. DCTdiff exhibits this ordering implicitly, whereas the proposed schedule explicitly incorporates spectral energy into the forward process through β k , t ( i ) \beta_{k,t}^{(i)} . A further distinction arises during sampling.
